title: Mujaddara
subtitle: Lentils and bulgur with crispy fried onions
excerpt: Mujaddara is a Levantine dish of lentils and bulgur wheat topped with a thick layer of dark, sweet fried onions. It is simple pantry food that takes about forty minutes and tastes far richer than the ingredient list suggests.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Mujaddara documented as one of the oldest and most widespread dishes in the Arab world, noted in medieval cookery manuscripts. Anissa Helou, Lebanese Cuisine (1994). The bulgur version described as more common in Syrian and Lebanese villages than the rice version.

recipe.batchNotes: Doubles easily. Keeps in the fridge for three days and tastes better the next day.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the full recipe the day before. The flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently with a splash of water.

content.text: Mujaddara is lentils and bulgur cooked together in spiced broth, finished with a crown of deeply fried onions that are taken past golden to a dark, jammy sweetness. The fried onions are not a garnish; they are half the dish, and they need patience: low heat and thirty minutes to reach the right colour. Serve with plain yoghurt and a green salad.
Heat 2 tablespoons of {{olive-oil}} in a large saucepan over a medium heat. Add the two finely chopped {{onion}} halves of the quantity and fry for ten minutes, stirring, until soft and golden.

Stir in {{cumin-ground}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, and {{allspice}} and cook for one minute. Add {{lentils-green}} and 800 ml of water. Bring to the boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for 20 minutes until the lentils are just tender.

Stir {{bulgur-wheat}} and {{sea-salt-fine}} into the lentil pot. The liquid should just cover the grain; add a splash more water if needed. Cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes until the bulgur is tender and has absorbed the liquid. Turn off the heat and leave, covered, for five minutes.

While the bulgur cooks, heat 3 tablespoons of {{olive-oil}} in a wide frying pan over a medium-low heat. Add the two thinly sliced {{onion}} halves of the quantity. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 25 to 30 minutes until the onions are very dark brown and caramelised. They should be almost crispy at the edges. Season with a pinch of salt.
Fluff the bulgur and lentil mixture with a fork. Spoon into a serving bowl or onto a large plate. Top with the fried onions and serve with {{plain-yoghurt}} alongside.

items.symptom: The bulgur is still hard in the middle after cooking
items.cause: Not enough liquid or the lid was not sealed tightly enough
items.fix: Add 50 ml of boiling water, replace the lid, and steam on the lowest heat for another ten minutes. The grain absorbs moisture slowly.

items.symptom: The lentils have gone mushy before the bulgur is added
items.cause: Cooked for too long or at too high a heat
items.fix: They should still have a little bite when you add the bulgur. They will soften further as the grain cooks. Start checking at 18 minutes.

items.symptom: The fried onions are golden but not dark enough
items.cause: Heat was too high so they coloured quickly without caramelising
items.fix: Lower the heat and keep cooking. The dark, jammy stage requires patience. They should be dark brown, not burnt.

items.cause: Under-seasoned or the onions did not caramelise fully
items.fix: Salt generously throughout: the lentils, the bulgur, and the onions. The caramelised onion sweetness is essential to the balance.

content.text: Mujaddara is one of the oldest dishes in the Arab world. A version appears in medieval cookery texts from the 13th century, and the lentil and grain pairing is old enough to have a link to the biblical mess of pottage. It is a dish built from cheap pantry staples that tastes far better than the ingredient list suggests. Across Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Palestine, and Egypt, the recipe varies: some use rice instead of bulgur, some add whole cumin seeds, some use green lentils and some brown. The dark fried onion topping is always there and cannot be left out.
